Article.ArticleTitle: Follow-Up Questionnaires in Pharmacovigilance: A Quantitative Evaluation Based on Completeness Score.

Abstract.AbstractText: Follow-up questionnaires (FUQs) are routinely used in pharmacovigilance to gather further information on suspected adverse drug reactions (ADRs) and are frequently included within Risk Management Plans. However, despite their extensive use and regulatory relevance, their contribution to improving the quality and completeness of case reports has not previously been evaluated quantitatively. The objective of this study was to assess whether the recommendation to implement or discontinue a FUQ was associated with changes in the completeness of information in case reports.

The minutes from January 2018 to July 2025 from the European Medicines Agency Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) were screened to identify recommendations regarding FUQ implementation or discontinuation. For active substance-ADR combinations associated with a FUQ recommendation, case reports and a standardised measure of report completeness were obtained from EudraVigilance and VigiBase, the WHO global database of adverse event reports for medicines and vaccines, respectively. Interrupted time series analyses were conducted to assess the effect of specific FUQs on the quality of case reporting.

Across the 27 active substance-ADR combinations evaluated, the impact of FUQs on report completeness was heterogeneous. Only six combinations showed statistically significant trend changes, of which one demonstrated a small improvement in completeness after FUQ implementation and five showed declining trends following implementation (n = 1) or discontinuation (n = 4).

The present findings do not support a consistent association between FUQ implementation and improved case completeness. Other factors, including ADR-related characteristics and heterogeneity in pharmacovigilance data collection practices, may be more important determinants of report quality. These findings provide the first quantitative evidence on FUQ effectiveness and support a more evidence-based approach to their evaluation within pharmacovigilance systems.

MeshHeading.DescriptorName: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

OtherAbstract.AbstractText: Follow‐up questionnaires (FUQs) are widely used in pharmacovigilance to collect additional information about suspected adverse drug reactions (ADRs). Despite their widespread use, little evidence has been available on whether they improve the quality of safety reports. This study evaluated the impact of recommendations to implement or discontinue FUQs on the completeness of case reports. Recommendations identified in the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) minutes between 2018 and 2025 were linked to reporting data from major international pharmacovigilance databases and analysed using interrupted time series methods. A total of 27 active substance‐ADR combinations were evaluated. The results showed that the effects of FUQs were variable and generally limited. Only a small number of combinations demonstrated statistically significant changes in report completeness and improvements following FUQ implementation were uncommon. Overall, the findings do not support a consistent association between FUQ use and increased completeness of case reports. These results suggest that factors such as the nature of the ADR and differences in reporting practices may play a greater role in determining report quality and highlight the importance of adopting a more evidence‐based approach to evaluating FUQs in pharmacovigilance.
